draft.title: Conditional probability from a two-way table
card: A two-way table sorts people or things by two features at once. Each cell counts those with both features.
When a condition is given, only the row or column for that condition counts. That row or column total becomes the new total.
Probability given the condition = number with both features ÷ total for the condition. Do not use the grand total.
Example: 40 students, 24 take the bus and 16 do not. Of the 24 bus riders, 6 are in Year 7. P(Year 7 given bus) = 6/24 = 1/4.
draft.remember: Given a condition, shrink the total to that row or column.

a.q: A table shows 30 members of a club. 18 are juniors, and 12 of the juniors play netball. What is P(plays netball given junior)?
a.why: The condition is junior, so the total is the 18 juniors. 12 of them play netball, giving 12/18. Using 30 would divide by everyone, which ignores the condition.
a.clue: Which group are we told about?

b.q: At a Perth school, 50 students were asked about a sport. 20 play football, and 8 of those also play cricket. 15 play cricket but not football. What is P(football given cricket)?
b.why: Cricket players are 8 + 15 = 23, so that is the total. Of them, 8 play football, giving 8/23. The tempting 8/20 uses the football total, which reverses the condition.
b.clue: Find the total for the group named after the word given.

check.summary: No problems found. Both answers (12/18 and 8/23) are correct, the card's example is accurate, and the distractors are fair.

final.title: Conditional probability from a two-way table
card: A two-way table sorts people or things by two features at once. Each cell counts those with both features.
When a condition is given, only the row or column for that condition counts. That row or column total becomes the new total.
Probability given the condition \(=\) number with both features \(\div\) total for the condition. Do not use the grand total.
Example: 40 students, 24 take the bus and 16 do not. Of the 24 bus riders, 6 are in Year 7. \(P(\text{Year 7 given bus}) = \frac{6}{24} = \frac{1}{4}\).

a.why: The condition is junior, so the total is the 18 juniors. 12 of them play netball, giving \(\frac{12}{18}\). Using 30 would divide by everyone, which ignores the condition.
a.clue: Which group are we told about?

b.q: At a Perth school, 50 students were asked about a sport. 20 play football, and 8 of those also play cricket. 15 play cricket but not football. What is \(P(\text{football given cricket})\)?
b.why: Cricket players are \(8 + 15 = 23\), so that is the total. Of them, 8 play football, giving \(\frac{8}{23}\). The tempting \(\frac{8}{20}\) uses the football total, which reverses the condition.
b.clue: Find the total for the group named after the word given.
